stem: A refund agent handles long chat sessions and uses progressive summarization to keep its context small. In one 45-turn session the customer first said the amount was $159.99, the order lookup tool returned $149.99, and the policy window stood at day 28 of 30. After two summarization passes the agent re-asked for the amount and then quoted $159.99. The team wants a fix that keeps context compact without depending on what the summarizer chooses to keep. Which change best addresses this?
options: Move to a model with a larger context window so the whole session fits and summarization never has to run.
Keep progressive summarization but instruct the summarizer to preserve every amount, date, and policy detail it judges important.
Keep a compact block of tool-confirmed facts (order ID, amount, policy-window day) pinned at the top of context, refreshed each turn.
Keep a compact block of facts updated from each customer message as it arrives, so the latest stated values stay pinned at the top of context.
explanation: Summarization that drops amounts, dates, and policy thresholds is a reliability bug, and identifiers and exact figures are the first things a model-written summary loses. Extracting transactional facts into a compact block at the top of context removes the dependency on the summarizer and also keeps them out of the low-attention middle. The block must hold verified tool data, which is what distinguishes the best answer from the near-miss that would pin the customer's wrong figure.
whyWrong: A bigger window raises the ceiling but does not make attention uniform or remove the need for extraction; the same loss reappears later in a longer session.
This still relies on a lossy, model-chosen summary. An instruction improves the odds but does not guarantee the figure survives.
Correct: verified, compact, top-placed and refreshed facts survive summarization and the lost-in-the-middle effect without depending on the summarizer.
Right structure, wrong source. The block holds confirmed tool data, never unverified customer claims, so here it would pin the wrong $159.99.
concept: case-facts block of verified transactional facts
plainExample: A call-centre agent writes the confirmed order number, refund amount and deadline on a sticky note at the top of her screen, copied from the order system rather than from what the caller half-remembers. However long the call runs, she glances at the note instead of trying to recall a figure from twenty minutes ago.
technicalExample:
CASE_FACTS (top of context, rewritten every turn, under 200 tokens)
{ "customer_id": "8841", "order_id": "#29384",
  "refund_amount": "$149.99", "amount_source": "orders_get",
  "policy_window": "day 28 of 30" }
Customer-stated $159.99 is NOT written here: tool-confirmed values only.
Wrong: summary reads 'Customer reported delivery issues, requesting refund.' (amount and deadline gone)

stem: A CI job runs a Claude agent that triages failing test suites. Each test-runner call returns about 20,000 tokens of log output, of which the agent needs only the failing test names, file paths, line numbers, and assertion messages. After five or six calls the agent starts attributing failures to the wrong test files. The team has a fixed per-run token budget and must keep the full logs available for later audit. Which change best fixes this?
options: Enable server-side tool-result clearing so the oldest log outputs are dropped from context automatically once a token threshold is passed.
Add a post-tool hook that keeps only failing test IDs, paths, and messages in context, saving each raw log as an artifact referenced by path.
Enable server-side compaction so the accumulated log output is summarized automatically into a short narrative once the session crosses the trigger.
Raise the maximum output tokens so the agent has more room to reason across all of the verbose log output it has collected during the run.
explanation: Untrimmed tool output is the dominant cause of context bloat, and the fix is to trim it before it accumulates rather than clean up afterward. Extracting the identifiers the next step needs keeps the context small and accurate, and recording the artifact path makes the trimming reversible, which satisfies the audit constraint. Clearing and compaction both act after the bloat and each loses identifiers in its own way.
whyWrong: Clearing removes content outright, so an identifier that lived only in a cleared log is gone rather than blurred, and nothing points back to the raw output.
Correct: trims at the hook layer before accumulation, keeps exact identifiers, and keeps a path to the raw log so nothing is unrecoverable.
Compaction is a lossy, model-written summary; file paths and test identifiers are exactly the details that degrade first.
The output budget is separate from input context. More room to write does nothing about the 95 percent noise the agent is reading.
concept: trim tool output at the hook layer and keep a path to raw output
plainExample: A clerk gets a 40-page delivery report every morning but needs only four lines from it. Instead of stacking every full report on her desk until she cannot find anything, she copies the four lines onto an index card, files the report in a cabinet, and writes the drawer number on the card.
technicalExample:
PostToolUse(run_tests) -> updatedToolOutput:
FAILURES run-4812   raw_log: artifacts/run-4812/test.log
  t-01 tests/billing/test_invoice.py:88   AssertionError: expected 1250 got 1249
  t-02 tests/cart/test_totals.py:141      TimeoutError after 30s
About 60 tokens reach context instead of about 20,000; the full log is one read away.
Wrong: keep every raw log verbatim, or clear it with no pointer back.

stem: A developer has spent four hours in one Claude Code session investigating a flaky build tool. The investigation is finished and the work has moved to implementing a fix, but the history is full of abandoned hypotheses and the agent keeps reverting to an approach the developer ruled out two hours ago. The developer wants the implementation phase to start clean without losing two locked decisions and the exact file paths identified. What is the best move?
options: Keep working in the same session and add a strongly worded reminder that the ruled-out approach must not be used again.
Trigger compaction on the current session so the investigation history is summarized and the implementation work continues from that summary.
Switch to a model with a larger context window so the earlier corrections stay visible alongside the rest of the history.
Start a fresh session with a handoff brief carrying the locked decisions, the ruled-out approach, and the exact file paths.
explanation: When the task has changed phase and the history is more contradiction than context, a fresh session with a handoff brief is the preservation strategy that fits. It has the highest one-off authoring cost and the cheapest steady state, and its risk is that anything not in the brief is gone, so the brief must carry the decisions, the exclusion, and the identifiers verbatim. Compaction would carry a model-chosen version of the contradictory narrative forward.
whyWrong: Another sentence competes with hours of contradictory history, and a prompt instruction is the first thing lost; it removes none of the contradiction.
Compaction suits a session where the reasoning path matters. Here the path is mostly abandoned hypotheses, and a model-chosen summary may keep them and blur the paths.
A bigger window keeps all the contradictory material in view and does nothing for density; the reverting behavior stays.
Correct: phase change plus contradictory history is the case for a fresh start, and the brief carries forward exactly what must survive.
concept: fresh session with handoff brief when history is more contradiction than context
plainExample: After a long brainstorming meeting where half the ideas were rejected, you do not hand the builder the full meeting recording. You give them a one-page work order: what was decided, what was ruled out, and the exact addresses they need. Whatever is not on the page will not reach them, so you write it carefully.
technicalExample:
HANDOFF BRIEF (new session)
locked: D1 pin toolchain to cache key v3; D2 no edits to ci/matrix.yml
ruled_out: disabling the remote cache (breaks release builds)
paths: build/cache/key.ts:40-72, scripts/warm-cache.sh
hypotheses_to_validate: race in warm-cache.sh (unconfirmed)
Wrong: compact the 4-hour history and hope the summary drops the abandoned approach.

stem: A support agent escalates any ticket whose sentiment classifier score is strongly negative. The human queue is now overloaded with angry customers whose refunds were fully covered by policy, while a case where no playbook covered a partial refund on a bundled item was handled automatically with a guessed amount. The support lead wants fewer escalations and fewer unsafe automated actions. Which change best achieves both?
options: Escalate only on checkable triggers (an explicit request for a human, a policy gap, or no progress) and resolve covered cases even if the customer is upset.
Raise the sentiment threshold so that only the most extreme negative messages escalate, and add a policy-gap check as a secondary escalation signal.
Add a self-assessed confidence score and escalate whenever the agent rates its own confidence below 7 out of 10, keeping the sentiment trigger as well.
Escalate any ticket that needs more than three tool lookups or more than two policy conditions, since complexity predicts where the agent is likely to fail.
explanation: Sentiment, complexity, and self-reported confidence are all unreliable proxies for whether a human is needed. The valid triggers are an explicit request for a human, a policy gap, and genuine inability to progress, each checkable against the record, and policy-covered cases should be resolved even when the customer is frustrated. That single change cuts the angry-but-covered volume and catches the uncovered bundle case.
whyWrong: Correct: checkable triggers remove the sentiment-driven volume and route the policy-gap case to a human instead of a guess.
Tuning the threshold on an unreliable proxy still escalates on mood; the policy-gap check is right but demoted to a secondary signal.
Self-reported confidence is noise rather than a calibrated signal, and formalizing it into a 1-to-10 rating keeps the volatility.
Complexity alone is not a trigger; several conditions and lookups are solvable by the agent and call for care, not handoff.
concept: escalate on checkable criteria, not sentiment, complexity, or confidence
plainExample: A shop manager who tells staff to call her whenever a customer sounds angry spends all day on easy returns, while a genuinely unusual case slips through because a clerk improvised. A rule like 'call me when the customer asks for me, when our policy does not cover it, or when you have tried everything' gets her to the right cases.
technicalExample:
Wrong: if sentiment(msg) < -0.6: escalate()
Right (evaluate in order, record the matched rule id):
E1 customer explicitly asks for a human      -> escalate now, no automated reply
A1 no playbook matches OR playbooks conflict -> escalate, reason=policy_gap
S1 tools exhausted, no progress              -> escalate, reason=stuck
P1 playbook matches, required fields present -> resolve (frustration alone is not a trigger)

stem: A customer writes 'Please refund my order, it arrived broken.' The account has two orders delivered this week, and the refund playbook requires an order ID; everything else the playbook needs is already present. The design goal is to resolve the ticket without guessing and without pushing extra work onto the customer. Which TWO behaviors should the agent's rules specify? (Select TWO.)
options: Refund the most recently delivered order, since it is the most likely match, and state the order ID in the confirmation message.
Ask one clarifying question that names both candidate orders and asks which one arrived broken, then re-evaluate the rules.
Escalate to a human immediately, because any ambiguity in the request means the agent is uncertain and should not act on it.
If the customer's reply is still ambiguous, route the ticket to a human instead of asking a second clarifying question.
Collect the order ID, damage photos, preferred refund method, and a reason code in one message before looking anything up.
explanation: When exactly one required field is missing and the customer can supply it, the right move is one clarifying question, then re-evaluation. The clarification budget is capped at one per ticket, and a second ambiguity escalates, because questions are cheap individually and corrosive in aggregate. Guessing risks a confident wrong refund, and escalating immediately is over-escalation.
whyWrong: Guessing on a money-moving action produces a confident wrong refund that the customer finds, not you.
Correct: exactly one missing field that the customer can supply is the case for a single, specific clarifying question.
Over-escalation: one resolvable missing field is not a reason for a human, and a flooded queue leads reviewers to rubber-stamp.
Correct: the one-question budget prevents an interrogation loop, and a second ambiguity routes to a human.
Interrogation: it asks for fields the playbook does not need and moves work onto the customer while still charging them the latency.
concept: bounded clarification: one question, then escalate
plainExample: A waiter hears 'I'll have the special' on a night with two specials. He asks once, 'the fish or the risotto?', rather than guessing or firing off ten questions. If the answer is still unclear, he fetches the manager rather than turning dinner into an interview.
technicalExample:
Q1 ASK ONE CLARIFYING QUESTION, then re-evaluate
  when: playbook matches AND exactly one required field missing AND customer can supply it
  ask:  'Was it ORD-5512 (lamp) or ORD-5519 (mug) that arrived broken?'
  limit: one per ticket; a second ambiguity routes to a human
Wrong: default to the newest order, or ask for four fields the ticket does not need.

stem: A damaged item bought in a clearance sale matches two playbooks: the warranty playbook says replace it, and the clearance playbook says final sale, store credit only. The current agent applies whichever playbook it matched first and sends the customer a confirmation. Leadership wants each such case handled safely and also wants to learn how often the policy itself is incomplete. What should the agent do?
options: Apply the playbook with the lower cost to the company, since conflicts should default to the most conservative financial outcome.
Ask the customer whether they would prefer a replacement or store credit, and then apply whichever playbook matches their answer.
Abstain: route it to the human queue as a policy_gap with both playbooks attached, and review that queue weekly to revise the policy.
Escalate to a human and, in the meantime, send the customer a reply saying the replacement has been approved and is now being arranged.
explanation: Two playbooks matching with conflicting actions is a policy gap, not a request ambiguity, so the correct path is abstention to a human with a policy_gap reason. Attaching the playbooks considered makes the case fast to decide, and reviewing that queue weekly is what reveals where the policy is incomplete, which is leadership's second goal. Guessing, or asking the customer to pick, hides the gap.
whyWrong: This is still a guess at a policy decision the agent has no rule for, and it hides the gap from the policy review.
A clarifying question masks the real problem when the ambiguity is in the policy rather than the request; the customer cannot settle a policy conflict.
Correct: the abstention path both routes the case safely and produces the evidence of a policy gap.
Escalating is right, but a holding reply that implies resolution is explicitly prohibited and misleads the customer.
concept: abstention path that files a policy gap
plainExample: A new cashier finds two store rules that contradict each other for one return. Quietly picking one, or asking the customer which rule they like better, both hide the problem. The right move is to call the supervisor and add the case to a list the manager reads every week, so the rulebook gets fixed.
technicalExample:
A1 ABSTAIN AND FILE A POLICY GAP
  trigger: two playbooks match with conflicting actions
  route:   human queue, reason='policy_gap'
  attach:  ticket, playbooks=[warranty_v3, clearance_final_sale], undecided='replace vs store credit'
  never:   guess, or send a holding reply that implies resolution
  A1 volume reviewed weekly -> input to the next policy revision

stem: A research coordinator fans out five search subagents. Two of them hit upstream timeouts, catch the exception, and return an empty findings list with status 'success'. The synthesis step then reports that no published evidence was found for the two subtopics those subagents covered. The team wants the smallest change that stops these false negatives while keeping the three good results. What is the best fix?
options: Instruct the synthesis agent to lower its stated confidence and add a caveat whenever a subtopic returns noticeably fewer findings than the others.
Have the coordinator discard the run and restart all five subagents from scratch whenever any subagent returns fewer results than expected.
Increase the subagent timeout and have each subagent keep retrying every failed search until it returns at least one result to the coordinator.
Have subagents return failures distinctly from empty results, with error class, retryability, and coverage counts, for the coordinator to act on.
explanation: The root cause is that a failure crossed the agent boundary looking identical to a genuine empty result, so the coordinator read 'not searched' as 'nothing found'. A structured return that separates what succeeded from what failed, classifies each failure, and carries coverage counts lets the coordinator keep the three good results, retry the transient failures within a bound, and propagate any remaining gap. Lowering confidence does not name the gap.
whyWrong: A confidence downgrade is not a substitute for naming the gap; a reader still treats the two subtopics as searched and empty.
Discarding three good results because two failed is the waste the partial-result contract exists to prevent.
Unbounded retries waste budget, and 'until at least one result' pressures the system to manufacture findings where a true empty was possible.
Correct: distinguishing an empty result from a failure, with class, retryability, and coverage, turns the coordinator's choice into routing.
concept: empty result is not success: structured failure with coverage
plainExample: Three people are sent to check eight rooms for damp. One cannot get the key, and the report that comes back says 'no damp in the building'. The fix is not to make the report sound less sure; it is for that person to say 'rooms six and seven not entered, key missing', so someone can go back.
technicalExample:
Wrong: {"status": "success", "findings": []}    # the timeout was swallowed
Right:
{
  "status": "partial",
  "completed": {"subtopics": 3},
  "failures": [{"unit": "subtopic/cathode-reuse", "error_class": "transient",
                "error_code": "upstream_timeout", "retryable": true, "attempts": 3}],
  "coverage": {"requested": 5, "completed": 3},
  "claim_scope": "No findings for 2 subtopics means NOT searched, not absent."
}

stem: A CI pipeline's coordinator delegates dependency, licence, and secrets scans to three subagents. Each subagent invented its own failure labels, such as ACCESS_PROBLEM, flaky, blocked, and denied_maybe, and the coordinator keeps retrying authorization failures while escalating simple timeouts. The MCP tools the subagents call already classify their own errors. Which change most directly fixes the misrouting?
options: Have subagents report error_class with the tool layer's transient, business, and permission values, putting situational detail in error_code.
Let each subagent keep its own descriptive labels, and add a translation table in the coordinator that maps every label to a retry decision.
Have subagents return a plain-language description of each failure and let the coordinator's model decide what to do based on the wording.
Collapse every failure into a single retryable boolean flag, and have the coordinator retry anything marked retryable up to three times before escalating.
explanation: Reusing the tool layer's taxonomy at the agent layer means the coordinator routes on one vocabulary and never translates: transient gets a bounded retry, business changes the plan, and permission escalates. The situational detail, such as auth_denied or upstream_timeout, belongs in error_code for the human. A second vocabulary only adds a translation step that drifts as new labels appear.
whyWrong: Correct: one taxonomy across layers; error_class decides the action and error_code records what happened.
A translation table is exactly the cost a shared vocabulary avoids, and it breaks each time a subagent invents a new label.
An error that crosses an agent boundary as prose becomes a rumor; the coordinator cannot branch reliably on wording.
A single boolean loses the difference between business and permission failures, which are both non-retryable but need different actions.
concept: one error_class vocabulary across tool and agent layers
plainExample: If every hospital department used its own word for 'urgent', the triage desk would spend its day translating and still get some wrong. One shared set of labels, such as urgent, routine, and needs-authorization, lets the desk route instantly, while a notes field keeps the detail for the doctor.

stem: A contract-extraction coordinator sends 40 contracts to extraction subagents. One subagent returns a well-formed partial result: 36 contracts extracted and 4 failed on unreadable scans, with a claim_scope stating those 4 were not examined. The coordinator's summary to the legal team reads 'No change-of-control clauses found across the 40 contracts.' Where is the defect, and what fixes it?
options: In the subagent: it should have kept retrying the four unreadable scans until extraction succeeded before returning any result.
In the coordinator: it absorbed the coverage gap; its summary must say 36 of 40, name the four contracts, and say why.
In the wording: the coordinator should add 'medium confidence' to its report whenever any subagent returns a partial status.
In the orchestration: the coordinator should re-extract all 40 contracts itself so it no longer depends on subagent coverage reports.
explanation: The subagent did its job; the gap disappeared one level up, when the coordinator turned 36 examined contracts into a claim about 40. Error propagation that stops one level short of the human is laundering, so the coordinator must carry coverage counts and the named gaps into the legal team's summary. Legal teams act on absence of findings, which makes this a reliability defect rather than a wording issue.
whyWrong: An unreadable scan will fail the same way every time, so retrying does not help, and the subagent already reported the gap correctly.
Correct: the coordinator must propagate the coverage gap into human-facing output rather than absorb it.
A confidence downgrade does not say which four contracts were skipped; the team would still treat them as clean.
A coordinator that re-reads what its subagents read pays full cost twice, and it still would not fix how the gap is reported.
concept: coordinator must propagate coverage gaps to the human
plainExample: A team assistant receives a note saying '36 of 40 files checked, 4 were illegible', then tells the boss 'none of the 40 files had the problem'. Every word the assistant received was accurate, yet the gap vanished at the last step. The message to the boss has to keep '36 of 40' and name the four files.
technicalExample:
Subagent result (correct):
{"coverage": {"requested": 40, "completed": 36, "failed": 4},
 "claim_scope": "C-07, C-19, C-22, C-31 NOT examined (unreadable scan)"}

Coordinator report (wrong):
  "No change-of-control clauses found across the 40 contracts."
Coordinator report (right):
  "None found in 36 of 40. C-07, C-19, C-22, C-31 were not examined
   (unreadable scans); absence of findings there is not evidence they are clean."

stem: Before a refactor, a developer asks Claude Code to find every call site of a deprecated chargeCard() function in a 3,000-file monorepo. The first attempt read the payments directory file by file and had used most of the context window before the refactor even started. The developer needs a complete list and a main session that still has room for the implementation. Which approach is best?
options: Read the payments and billing directories in full first, since most call sites are likely to live there, and then search the rest of the repository.
Rely on the large context window and load all of the repository's source files into the session at once so that no call site can possibly be missed.
Search for the symbol to get paths and line numbers, read only the matched ranges, and delegate the wide sweep to a subagent returning file:line hits.
List every source file in the repository, then read each one in turn and keep a running prose summary of anything that looks related to payments.
explanation: Exploration is a retrieval problem: a symbol search covers the whole corpus cheaply and returns a map of paths and line numbers, and only the matched ranges need to be read. Delegating the wide sweep to a subagent lets the exploration cost accrue in a context that is discarded, so the main session keeps its room for the refactor. The return contract of file:line identifiers is what makes the delegation worth paying for.
whyWrong: Reading whole files has terrible density, crowds out later work, and gives no completeness guarantee for call sites outside those directories.
Loading everything maximizes cost and minimizes density, and recall degrades as the window fills even when it fits.
Correct: search-then-read keeps identifiers rather than content, and the subagent absorbs the exploration cost.
A linear scan has no upper bound on cost, and running prose summaries drop the exact paths and line numbers the refactor needs.
concept: search-then-read and subagent delegation for codebase exploration
plainExample: To find which of 400 supplier contracts mention one company, you search the index first, get a list of contract and clause numbers, then read just those clauses. Reading all 400 contracts cover to cover leaves you exhausted and still unsure you caught them all.
technicalExample:
1 Grep 'chargeCard(' -> 23 hits in 17 files (paths + line numbers = the map)
2 Read each matched range plus about 15 lines to establish scope
3 Follow one level of callers of any wrapper found
4 Subagent returns: 'src/checkout/pay.ts:118, src/subs/renew.ts:44, ... (23 sites)'
Wrong: Read(payments/*) in full -> most of the window gone before the real question.

stem: An internal developer tool uses an exploration subagent, run as a forked-context skill, to answer 'why do some legacy endpoints skip authentication?'. The subagent returns 'Authentication looks mostly fine; a few legacy handlers might be worth a look.' The main session then re-reads the handler files itself, roughly doubling the cost of every investigation. Which change best fixes this?
options: Specify the subagent's return contract: exact files and line ranges, the bypass path, the test that would catch it, and what went unexamined.
Drop the subagent entirely and let the main session explore the handlers directly, since it ends up reading the same files anyway.
Keep the design, but have the main session always re-read every file the subagent read so that the subagent's conclusions are verified.
Run the subagent on a larger, more capable model so its summaries are more thorough and the main session can trust them without re-reading files.
explanation: The value of delegating exploration is entirely in what comes back: exact files, line ranges, and identifiers can stand in for tens of thousands of tokens, while 'looks mostly fine' spent the same money and bought nothing. Writing the return contract into the delegation removes the reason the main session re-reads. Dropping the subagent or re-reading everything throws away the context isolation that justified it.
whyWrong: Correct: a specified return contract makes the subagent's conclusion actionable without redoing the work.
This gives up the discarded exploration context, so the main window fills with the handler files the subagent existed to keep out.
A coordinator that re-reads what its subagent read pays full cost twice; this is a named anti-pattern, not verification.
A larger model does not fix an unspecified return shape; a more fluent impression still lacks paths and line numbers.
concept: write the subagent return contract before delegating
plainExample: You send an assistant to the archive. If they come back saying 'it all looked fine, mostly', you have to go yourself, and the trip was wasted. If you tell them up front to bring back file numbers, page numbers, and what they did not get to, their trip replaces yours.
technicalExample:
Return contract (written into the delegation prompt):
  files_and_ranges, finding, bypass_path, test_that_would_catch_it, not_examined
Good: 'Auth enforced in middleware/auth.go:44-91. handlers/legacy.go:120,188,203 register via
  registerRaw(), skipping the middleware chain. Test: TestLegacyRequiresAuth. Not examined: grpc/.'
Bad:  'Authentication looks mostly fine.'

stem: An engineer uses Claude Code to assess the blast radius of renaming a widely used config loader in a large service repository. The current prompt pastes the diff plus the full contents of every file that imports the loader, about 60 files, and then asks for a risk review. Reviews of large changes keep missing issues in files near the middle of the pasted material. Which change best improves reliability?
options: Keep pasting the full file contents, but place them after the question so that the most recent material sits closest to the actual request.
Split the 60 files into batches of ten, review each batch in its own session, and concatenate the six reports at the end.
Paste only the ten most recently modified importing files, since recent changes are where regressions most often appear.
Keep the diff and the importing paths in context, search for the loader's call patterns, and read only matched ranges and direct callers.
explanation: Pasting 60 whole files is an attempt to hold the corpus in the window instead of querying it, and material in the middle of a long input is used least reliably. Keeping lightweight identifiers in context and pulling matched ranges through search is just-in-time retrieval, and knowing which files reference a symbol says more about blast radius than reading any one of them in full. The other options rearrange, shrink, or split the same flawed approach.
whyWrong: This contradicts the placement guidance, which puts bulk material first and the question last, and it does nothing about density.
Splitting breaks the cross-file reasoning a blast-radius review needs, because no batch can see interactions with the others.
Recency is a proxy, not retrieval; it guesses which files matter and misses importers that have not changed recently.
Correct: identifiers in context, content loaded just in time, and the reference map itself shows the blast radius.
concept: keep identifiers, not content; just-in-time retrieval
plainExample: To see who is affected by a changed office policy, you do not photocopy every employee's full file. You pull the list of people the policy applies to, then read the one relevant line in each file. The list alone tells you most of how far the change reaches.
technicalExample:
Context keeps: diff + importers list (60 paths, no bodies)
Grep 'loadConfig(' -> 142 call sites; Grep 'config.legacy.' -> 9 sites
Read each matched range plus about 20 lines; follow direct callers once
Record: 'risk: jobs/nightly.ts:77 reads legacy key removed in diff'
Wrong: paste 60 full files and ask one question at the end.

stem: An invoice-extraction pipeline will auto-post any extraction whose self-reported confidence is 0.9 or higher. The threshold was chosen after a random 200-document evaluation showed 95 percent accuracy overall. Volume is 80 percent native PDF invoices, 15 percent scanned receipts, and 5 percent handwritten delivery notes, and finance allows at most a 2 percent error rate on auto-posted items. What should the architect do before go-live?
options: Go live at 0.9, since 95 percent overall accuracy on a random sample already shows that the pipeline performs well across the whole document mix.
Label a sample stratified by document type, measure accuracy per confidence bucket in each type, and set per-type thresholds to the 2 percent target.
Raise the global threshold to 0.97 so that only the extractions the model is most certain about are posted without any human review at all.
Ask the model to justify each confidence score in one sentence, and auto-post only the items whose justification cites specific extracted fields.
explanation: Stated confidence is a claim, not a measured probability, until it has been bucketed against outcomes on a labelled sample, and the mapping often differs by input type. A random 200 documents contains only about ten handwritten notes, so the aggregate figure can hide a failing segment while barely moving. Stratifying by document type and setting per-type thresholds against the stated 2 percent target turns the threshold into a decision instead of a guess.
whyWrong: An aggregate over a mixed population hides the low-volume segment that fails, and the 0.9 threshold has never been checked against outcomes.
Correct: stratified labelled sampling plus per-bucket, per-type accuracy is what calibration means, and the threshold is then set to the stated target.
A higher global number is still uncalibrated; it raises review cost everywhere and may still admit a badly performing handwritten segment.
A self-justification comes from the same process as the confidence score; it establishes no relationship to observed correctness.
concept: calibrate thresholds on a labelled, stratified sample by document type
plainExample: A forecaster who says '90 percent chance of rain' only means it if, on the days they said 90, it rained about nine times in ten. And a train line that is 94 percent on time can still have one service that is late every morning. You check the forecaster's record, and you check each train separately.
technicalExample:
Stratified labelled sample (handwritten oversampled), illustrative figures:
type         items at >=0.9   observed accuracy   policy
native_pdf   400              99%                 auto-post at 0.9
scanned      300              97%                 auto-post only at a higher bucket
handwritten  150              61%                 always human review
Wrong: one global 0.9 chosen from 95% aggregate on 200 random documents.

stem: A claims-extraction pipeline has calibrated per-document-type thresholds, and only items below threshold go to human review. Reviewer capacity is fixed at about 10 percent of volume. A new insurer template starts arriving next quarter, and the team worries the thresholds will quietly go stale. Which addition best detects that drift without exceeding reviewer capacity?
options: Route every item to human review for the whole of next quarter so that any drift is caught directly on each item before it is posted.
Track the average stated confidence of auto-accepted items every week, and raise an alert if it drops below its historical baseline for any type.
Raise every threshold by a fixed safety margin as soon as the new template appears, so that more items fall into the human review queue.
Audit a stratified random sample of auto-accepted items per document type, oversampling the new template, and feed labels back into thresholds.
explanation: Thresholding gates individual items, but only sampling audits the population, including the items thresholding let through, which is the only way to see that a threshold has gone stale. A small stratified audit with the new template oversampled fits inside the fixed capacity, and feeding the labels back closes the loop. Confidently wrong items are exactly what a confidence-based monitor cannot see.
whyWrong: Full review blows the 10 percent capacity, and reviewer fatigue turns it into rubber-stamping, so measured accuracy drifts up while real accuracy does not.
Stated confidence can stay high while accuracy falls; average stated confidence is not a proxy for error rate.
A blanket margin is a global remedy without measurement; it raises cost in every segment and still produces no error rate.
Correct: sampling audits what the threshold passed, fits capacity, and feeds back into routing.
concept: stratified sampling audits what thresholding lets through
plainExample: A factory's automatic scanner waves through parts it is sure about. To know whether the scanner has started fooling itself, an inspector pulls a few approved parts off the line each day, from every product type, and checks them by hand. The scanner cannot catch its own blind spots; the spot checks can.
technicalExample:
Gate:  per-type threshold -> below threshold -> human review (about 7% of volume)
Audit: stratified random sample of AUTO-ACCEPTED items per type (about 2%)
       new_insurer_template stratum oversampled
Loop:  audit labels -> accuracy per confidence bucket -> reset thresholds
Wrong: watch average stated confidence; it stays high while accuracy falls.

stem: A multi-agent research system is launching to draft regulatory-change briefings that compliance officers file with a regulator. It is brand new, and there is no labelled data on its accuracy. Leadership wants to save reviewer time by auto-approving any briefing on which three independent agent runs agree. What review design should the architect recommend for launch?
options: Review every briefing at launch, recording verdicts to build the labelled set later needed for calibration and sampling.
Auto-approve briefings on which all three runs agree, and send only the disagreements to compliance officers for review.
Auto-approve briefings whose synthesis agent reports a confidence of 0.8 or higher, and send the rest to compliance officers for review.
Review a 5 percent random sample of briefings each week, and let the remaining briefings be filed with the regulator without review.
explanation: Regulated output, a brand-new pipeline, and no labelled data are each on their own a reason to review everything. Recording verdicts during that phase builds the labelled set that later justifies calibrated thresholds and stratified sampling, which is how full review stops being permanent. Agreement among runs that share the same criteria is not evidence of correctness.
whyWrong: Correct: full review fits regulated, new, unlabelled output, and the verdicts become the calibration data.
Unanimity across instances with the same flawed criteria is not correctness; shared blind spots agree too.
Self-reported confidence has not been measured against outcomes, so 0.8 is a number chosen for how it sounds.
Sampling measures the system but does not gate items, so individual bad briefings would still reach the regulator.
concept: review everything when regulated, new, and unlabelled
plainExample: A new hire's first reports to a regulator are all checked by a senior before they go out, and the senior keeps a tally of what was right. Only once that tally exists can the team decide which kinds of report are safe to spot-check. Three new hires agreeing with each other does not prove any of them is right.
technicalExample:
Launch (no labels, regulated output): review_all = true; log verdict per briefing
After enough labelled briefings: bucket by stated confidence and by jurisdiction; measure accuracy
Then: per-segment thresholds + stratified audit; keep full review where one error costs more than review
Wrong: auto-approve when 3 runs agree (runs sharing criteria share blind spots).

stem: A pipeline extracts figures from a company's annual report, two quarterly filings, and an analyst note into structured records, each carrying a source_id and page. A final merge step then writes a single company_profile paragraph for credit analysts. Analysts cannot tell which filing a revenue figure came from and end up re-reading all four documents. Which change best fixes this?
options: Append a bibliography of the four documents, with titles and dates, below the profile paragraph so analysts know what was consulted.
Instruct the merge step to write 'according to the filings' beside each figure, so readers know that every figure came from a source.
Have the merge step output claims and sources arrays linked by source_id, with a quote and page per claim, and render the prose from them.
Add an overall confidence rating to the profile paragraph so that analysts know how much weight to give to the figures it contains.
explanation: The provenance chain existed in the extracted records and broke at the merge step, because a stage that consumes structured data and outputs only prose destroys the claim-to-source links. Keeping claims and sources arrays intact, joined by a shared ID with a quote and locator, turns the analysts' review from re-derivation into spot-checking. A bibliography or confidence rating does not say which source supports which figure.
whyWrong: A bibliography lists what was read, not which source supports which claim, so the analyst still has to search all four.
Vague attribution without a specific source and locator is not verifiable and saves the reviewer nothing.
Correct: claim-level mapping through shared IDs, with quotes and locators, preserves provenance through synthesis.
A confidence rating does not tell the analyst where a figure came from, so it stays unverifiable.
plainExample: A student writes a strong essay from four books but loses track of which fact came from which book. When the teacher asks, the student has to re-read all four. Writing the book and page beside each fact as you go makes checking take seconds.

stem: A research system is asked for the size of the battery-recycling market. One subagent cites a 2024 industry report giving $12B; another cites a 2026 government statistics release giving $9B under a narrower definition. No source settles which definition the requester means, and no data was found for Southeast Asia. Which TWO elements belong in the synthesized output? (Select TWO.)
options: The 2026 figure reported as the answer, since it is the newer source, with the 2024 figure noted in a footnote as superseded.
Both claims with quote, locator, retrieval time, and source date, plus an unresolved conflict annotation naming the human decision needed.
Whichever figure most sources support, after the system searches for additional market reports to settle the disagreement.
The average of the two figures presented as a blended estimate, with both of the sources listed in the references section.
A coverage-gap statement that no Southeast Asia data was found, so that the absence is not read as a zero market there.
explanation: Given contradictory sources with no basis for choosing, any single figure is wrong as an output because it hides that there is no one answer. The output should carry both claims with their provenance and temporal details, annotate the conflict as unresolved with the human decision named, and state coverage gaps so silence is not read as a finding. Recency, majority vote, and averaging all resolve the conflict silently.
whyWrong: Recency is a heuristic about currency, not evidence about which source governs, and here the definitions also differ; the conflict disappears.
Correct: claim-source mapping, temporal handling, and conflict annotation with an explicit unresolved status.
Agreement among retrieved sources is not authority; adding sources to a definitional dispute produces a vote, not an answer.
An average is a number neither source supports, and it hides the disagreement behind a confident blend.
Correct: coverage gaps are part of the answer, because absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.
concept: annotate conflicts and coverage gaps instead of resolving silently
plainExample: A colleague asked for a deadline finds two emails with different dates. The helpful answer is: 'Procurement says the 15th, finance says the 20th; the finance email is newer but may cover a different step, so someone needs to confirm. And I found nothing about the Asia office.'

stem: A support knowledge assistant answers human agents' questions by combining policy PDFs with live results from the order-management tool. Compliance now requires every statement in an answer to be traceable to its exact source. The team has enabled the Citations feature on the policy documents only. What else is needed to meet the requirement?
options: Nothing further is needed, because the citations attached to the answer will also cover statements drawn from order-tool results.
Carry provenance for tool-derived statements in the team's own record structure: tool name, record ID, and retrieval time.
Instruct the model to write a page number in parentheses after every statement, including those based on order-tool results.
Paste the full text of each cited policy page into the answer so reviewers can check every statement against the original.
explanation: Citations configured on the policy documents return pointers into those documents, with the exact cited passage and a page location, but the order-tool results are not among the cited documents. Where citations do not apply, such as synthesis across tool results, provenance has to be carried in your own record structure. Prompt-based page numbers are less reliable than parsed citation pointers and mean nothing for a tool result.
whyWrong: The citations point into the documents they were enabled on; tool-derived statements are left with no source pointer.
Correct: document claims use citation objects, and tool-derived claims carry provenance in an explicit record.
Prompted page numbers are less reliable than parsed pointers, and an order-tool result has no page to cite.
Pasting whole pages bloats the answer without mapping any statement to its supporting passage.
concept: Citations for documents, own provenance records for tool results
plainExample: A reporter can footnote quotes from published reports with page numbers. For facts learned in a phone call there is no page, so the reporter logs who said it, when, and the call reference. Both kinds of fact need a trail, just a different kind of trail.
technicalExample:
Document claim: the API attaches a citation to the text block
{"type": "page_location", "cited_text": "Refunds within 30 days of delivery",
 "document_index": 0, "start_page_number": 4, "end_page_number": 5}

Tool claim: write your own provenance record
{"claim_id": "c3", "text": "ORD-7788 delivered 12 days ago",
 "source": {"tool": "orders_get", "record_id": "ORD-7788",
            "retrieved_at": "2026-09-29T10:14:00Z"}}

# Wrong: assuming the document citations also cover tool-result statements.
